title: Database Replication
concept: Replication keeps copies of a database on several machines so reads can spread out and a failed primary can be replaced. The hard questions are when a write counts as safe, on the primary alone or only once some copies have it, and how the system picks and announces a new primary without two machines accepting writes at once.

points: The hard questions are when a write counts as safe, and how to pick and announce a new primary without two machines accepting writes at once.
Meta put promotions and membership changes into the replication log, which it says gives provable safety across both.
GitHub gives each part one job, decides by quorum across data centers, and never depends on the failed node to help.

figures.label: typical failover about 2 s with Raft, 20 to 40 s with semi-synchronous replication
typical planned promotion takes about 300 ms

prerequisiteReasons.databases: Replication takes from databases the write-ahead log, since replicas stay current by replaying the primary's log in the same order.

posts.title: Building and deploying MySQL Raft at Meta

digest.problem: Meta's MySQL fleet used semi-synchronous replication to protect data, while promotions, failovers and changes of membership were handled by separate Python automation, locks, fencing and service discovery. Getting all of those to act together correctly was hard, corner cases kept piling up, and a failover took 20 to 40 seconds.
digest.constraints: The fleet holds millions of shards and petabytes on thousands of machines in regions on several continents, 10 to 100 ms apart. Services like the social graph need very fast commits, and semi-synchronous commits took under a millisecond. Meta chose to keep the binary log format, and the work started on MySQL 5.6 before moving to 8.0.

walkthrough.explanation: Meta forked the Raft implementation from Apache Kudu (kuduraft) and connected it to MySQL through a plugin, MyRaft.

walkthrough.step: Make the binary log the Raft log
walkthrough.explanation: Primaries and replicas write the binary log through Raft, replacing MySQL's separate relay log on replicas.

walkthrough.step: Commit on a small local quorum
walkthrough.explanation: A transaction waits for 2 of 3 votes in the leader's region, from the MySQL primary and two log-only members called logtailers, then commits. Other regions receive it without voting.
A variant called FlexiRaft keeps the commit quorum small and local, while a new leader's election must overlap the previous leader's region so no committed data is lost.

walkthrough.step: Put control actions in the log
walkthrough.explanation: Promotions and membership changes are written as entries in the same log, one membership change at a time.
Mock elections run before planned leadership transfers to avoid leaders getting stuck, and messages from members of a conflicting ring are refused.
Thousands of failovers and elections are injected on test rings before each release, and nightly checks compare primaries with replicas.

tradeoffs.chosen: Consensus inside the database: a small in-region quorum for commits, a larger quorum for elections, and every control action recorded in the replication log.
tradeoffs.rejected: Stock Raft with one global quorum, and automatic repair of a lost quorum. Joint consensus was not available in Kudu's Raft, and Meta only lists leaderless protocols as a speculative idea to explore.
tradeoffs.why: A global quorum would put a cross-region round trip on every commit. Kudu's Raft did not support joint consensus, so membership changes go one at a time. Repairing lost quorums by hand forces someone to find the cause instead of hiding it.

digest.failures: Raft made the system correct, but not more available on its own: two bad members in one region break the 2-of-3 quorum, so failed members have to be replaced quickly. Kudu's Raft had no automatic step-down, which allowed stuck leaders until mock elections were added. Provisioning races could create overlapping rings. Adapting the automation took several years, and turning Raft on caused a brief outage per ring.
digest.takeaways: Meta says putting promotions and membership changes into the replication log gave provable safety across them, after finding those operations triggered most issues. A small local quorum with a wider election quorum gives fast commits and fast failover together. Availability still depends on operations, and the tooling and testing cost as much as the server work.

posts.title: MySQL High Availability at GitHub
posts.ageNote: A 2018 account, updated in 2020, of an older approach: failover driven from outside the database by orchestrator. No newer GitHub post on MySQL failover is cited here, so GitHub's current setup may differ. GitHub's 2023 MySQL 8.0 post, on the Databases topic, still describes orchestrator running a planned failover. It is here as the contrast to Meta's consensus-based design.

digest.problem: GitHub's applications found each MySQL primary through a DNS name pointing to a virtual IP that the primary held. Moving that IP needed the old primary's cooperation, so a dead or unreachable primary could delay failover or leave two hosts claiming the same address, and a move to another data center needed a DNS change that clients had cached.
digest.constraints: GitHub ran several data centers and wanted to survive one being cut off, keep outages short, avoid losing data where possible, and limit split brain, where two servers accept writes at once. Failover could not depend on the failed primary doing anything.

walkthrough.explanation: Applications connect to one anycast writer address, which reaches the local HAProxy cluster. Each writer pool holds exactly one backend, the cluster's primary.
orchestrator watches the replication topology and notices the dead primary.
One or two orchestrator nodes per data center form a Raft group, so the leader makes the decision and an isolated data center cannot act alone.
orchestrator writes the new primary's identity to each data center's Consul store, and consul-template rewrites and reloads HAProxy.
A suitable replica is made writable and advertised before the rest of the replication tree is repaired.
Semi-synchronous replication makes the primary wait for a local replica to confirm each write, but only for 500 ms before carrying on alone.
A heartbeat tool runs on every server and writes only on the primary, so nothing has to be started or stopped during failover.

tradeoffs.chosen: Failover run from outside MySQL: orchestrator decides with Raft across data centers, Consul stores who the primary is, and proxies route writes.
tradeoffs.rejected: Virtual IPs and DNS for finding the primary, guaranteed lossless failover when a whole data center fails, and fully preventing split brain.
tradeoffs.why: Virtual IPs needed the failed host to cooperate and DNS changes waited on client caches. Losslessness on total data center loss and complete split-brain prevention were judged too expensive. A short semi-synchronous timeout trades a little safety for availability. A cost the post lists is that the proxies hide which client sent a query.

digest.failures: If the primary's data center is cut off, applications there can keep writing to it, risking diverging data; a way to shut it down from inside the isolated data center was still being worked on. Old connections linger for a while after failover, leaving a short split-brain window. A Consul outage during failover and partial isolation of a data center were not handled. The heartbeat tool needed patches to cope with servers switching between read-only and writable.
digest.takeaways: Give each part one job: one decides, one stores who the primary is, one routes traffic. Never depend on the failed node to help. Make decisions by quorum across data centers. Tune short timeouts deliberately, because they decide how much data safety you trade for availability.

comparison:
Both companies run MySQL with one primary per dataset and copies in several places, and both wait for another copy to confirm a write before treating it as safe, GitHub only up to a 500 ms timeout.

GitHub's 2018 setup, the older approach, kept MySQL's replication as it was and handled failover from outside: orchestrator detects the failure, agrees with Raft across data centers, and announces the new primary through Consul and HAProxy, with outages of 10 to 13 seconds.

Meta moved the decision inside the replication log with Raft, so commits, elections and membership changes are all entries in one log, cutting failover to about 2 seconds (a different measure from GitHub's total outage time), at the cost of years of automation work and a local quorum that two bad members can break.

glossary.definition: The primary waits for at least one replica to confirm it received a write, usually up to a timeout, before reporting success.
The number of members that must agree before a write or decision counts.
Replacing a failed primary with a replica and pointing clients at it.
Two servers both accepting writes for the same data, so their copies diverge.
A consensus algorithm that elects a leader and keeps a replicated log consistent across members.
How far a replica is behind the primary.

mistakes: Assuming failover is as fast as detection. Telling clients about the new primary can take longer, as GitHub found with DNS changes waiting on client caches.
Building failover that needs the failed primary to cooperate, such as releasing a shared IP address. A dead or cut-off host cannot help.
Expecting consensus alone to improve availability. Meta found Raft made failover correct and fast, but availability still depended on replacing failed members quickly.

why.outcome: After this you can explain why one copy of a database is not enough.
why.body:
A single database machine is a single point of failure. If it dies, writes stop, and anything not yet on another machine may be lost. It also has a limit on how many reads it can serve.

Replication keeps copies on several machines, so reads can spread out and a failed primary can be replaced. The hard part is not copying the data; it is deciding when a write counts as safe and how to switch to a new primary without two machines accepting writes at once.

mentalModel.outcome: After this you can picture a primary, its replicas, and what happens when the primary fails.
mentalModel.body:
One machine, the primary, accepts writes and ships its log to replicas. A commit can count as soon as the primary has it, which is fast but can lose data in a failover, or only once some replicas confirm it, which is safer but slower.

When the primary fails, three things must happen: someone notices, someone decides which replica becomes the new primary, and every client learns where to send writes. If two machines both think they are primary, split brain, they accept conflicting writes.

howItWorks.outcome: After this you can walk through a replicated write and a failover step by step.

steps.explanation: Clients send writes to the one primary, which appends them to its log.
Replicas receive the log and apply it in order. How far behind they are is replication lag.
Asynchronous: commit on the primary alone. Semi-synchronous: wait for at least one replica to confirm. Quorum: wait for a majority.
Heartbeats or a watcher notice the primary is gone.
A replica with the latest data is chosen, ideally by a quorum so an isolated part of the system cannot decide alone.
Clients learn the new primary through service discovery or proxies. Until they do, writes fail, and a reachable old primary must be stopped from accepting writes.

orchestrator writes the new primary to Consul, and HAProxy is rewritten to route writes there. A typical outage was 10 to 13 seconds.
GitHub's primary waited for one replica to confirm each write, but only for 500 ms, trading a little safety for availability.
Meta put Raft inside MySQL, so commits, elections and membership changes are all entries in the replicated log.
A commit waits for 2 of 3 votes in the leader's region, while an election must overlap the old leader's region so no committed data is lost. Failover dropped from 20 to 40 seconds to about 2.

lesson.mistakesOutcome: After this you can avoid three replication mistakes.
lesson.checkOutcome: After this you can tell whether you understood the concept before reading the posts.

quiz.question: What is split brain?
options: A replica falling behind the primary, so its reads show older data than the primary's
A query split across replicas, each of which answers a different part of it
Two machines both accepting writes as primary
quiz.why: Conflicting writes on two primaries can diverge and be hard to reconcile.
wrong: That is not a failure mode.

quiz.question: With asynchronous replication, the primary dies right after a commit. What can happen?
options: The commit may be lost if no replica received it
The replica rejects all writes forever
quiz.why: The primary did not wait for any copy, so the newest commits may exist only on the dead machine.
wrong: Only waiting for confirmation protects recent commits.
A replica can be promoted and accept writes.

quiz.question: Why should a failover not depend on the failed primary's cooperation?
options: A dead or cut-off machine cannot help
The primary is always busy, so it cannot answer a promotion request in time
It slows reads, because every replica must ask the old primary before answering
quiz.why: Designs like a shared IP that the old primary must release fail exactly when needed.
wrong: Busy is not the issue; unreachable is.

quiz.question: Why do failover decisions use a quorum across data centers?
options: So an isolated data center cannot promote a primary on its own
Because one vote is always wrong
quiz.why: A majority decision stops a cut-off side from creating a second primary.
wrong: Quorums are about safety, not read speed.
The point is agreement, not distrust of a single vote.

quiz.question: Why keep replicas at all, beyond backups?
options: Because primaries cannot write, so every change has to be made on a replica first
To spread reads and replace a failed primary quickly
To make writes faster, since each write can be sent to the nearest replica
quiz.why: Copies serve reads and are ready to take over.
wrong: Waiting for replicas can make writes slower, not faster.

quiz.question: Meta's commits wait for 2 of 3 votes in the leader's region. Why only that region?
options: Other regions do not store data, so they have nothing to vote on
Raft forbids more votes, so a larger quorum would not be allowed to commit
To avoid a cross-region round trip on every commit
quiz.why: Regions are 10 to 100 ms apart; a local quorum keeps commits fast.
wrong: Other regions receive the data without voting.
Raft allows larger quorums; Meta chose a small local one.

lesson.postsOutcome: After this you can describe two ways to run failover: outside the database and inside its log.
lesson.differOutcome: After this you can explain what moving failover into the replication log buys and costs.
lesson.exercisesOutcome: After this you can apply the concept to an outage, design failover, and plan for ten times the scale.

exercises.prompt: After a failover, clients kept writing to the old primary for a minute because they found it through a DNS name. What do you change?
exercises.answer: Stop relying on cached DNS for the primary. Route writes through proxies that read the current primary from a store the failover updates, and make sure the old primary is fenced or set read-only.
exercises.tradeoffs: Proxies add a hop and a component to run; fencing needs reliable access to the old host or its network.
wrongAnswers: Lowering the DNS TTL and hoping.
Relying on the old primary to step down by itself.

exercises.prompt: Design failover for a database with replicas in three data centers.
exercises.answer: Detect failure with heartbeats, decide by quorum across data centers, promote the most up-to-date replica, publish the new primary to a store, and route clients through proxies that follow it. Choose how many replicas must confirm a commit, and how long to wait.
exercises.tradeoffs: Waiting for confirmations adds commit latency; a timeout trades safety for availability.
wrongAnswers: A single watcher that can decide alone.
Failover that needs the failed primary.
No plan for a cut-off data center.

exercises.prompt: You now run millions of shards across continents. What makes failover fast and correct at that size?
exercises.answer: Put commits, elections and membership changes in the replicated log itself, use a small local quorum for commits and a wider one for elections, inject failures in testing, and replace failed members quickly.
exercises.tradeoffs: Years of tooling work, and a local quorum that two bad members can break.
wrongAnswers: One global quorum, which adds a cross-region round trip to every commit.
Expecting consensus alone to raise availability.
Repairing lost quorums automatically without finding the cause.

next.outcome: After this you can pick the next topic that builds on this one.
next.body: Every replica still holds all the data, so replication cannot help a table that is too big or too busy for one machine. Sharding picks up from there, building on Consistent Hashing as well. Object Storage is a later case of the same idea: keeping objects safe across many drives with copies and erasure coding. Disaster Recovery and Backups covers what replication cannot do: bring back data that a mistake or corruption damaged on every replica at once.
